title: 502 Bad Gateway across Payment API after deployment
error_message: 502 Bad Gateway: upstream timed out while connecting to backend
symptoms: Requests intermittently failing immediately following v2.4.1 deployment. Traffic dropping 40%.
logs: [error] 1421#1421: *892011 upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while connecting to upstream, client: 198.51.100.4, server: api.payments.internal, request: "POST /v1/charges HTTP/1.1", upstream: "http://10.0.4.15:8080/v1/charges", host: "api.payments.internal"
infrastructure_details: Kubernetes cluster us-east-1, AWS ALB -> Nginx Ingress Controller -> Gunicorn/Uvicorn Pods
additional_context: Deployment changed ingress keepalive timeout and upstream routing port mapping.

attempts.action: Restart Payment API service pods
attempts.hypothesis: Transient process deadlock or warm-up starvation
attempts.failure_reason: Pods restarted in 45s but 502 errors persisted at identical 40% error rate.
attempts.observed_result: Service restart did not alter the upstream connection timeout behavior.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting the backend pods was ineffective and added 30s of unnecessary pod termination overhead.

attempts.action: Increase proxy_read_timeout in Ingress to 120s
attempts.hypothesis: Upstream backend is taking longer to process under load
attempts.failure_reason: Connections still timed out; client latency ballooned from 2s to 120s, amplifying queue pileup.
attempts.observed_result: Increased client timeouts caused cascaded socket exhaustion on the ingress controller.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing timeout merely prolonged user wait time; the backend was never receiving packets.

attempts.action: Correct upstream configuration and keepalive mismatch in Ingress ConfigMap
attempts.hypothesis: Nginx upstream block pointed to stale container port 8080 instead of newly mapped targetPort 8000.
attempts.observed_result: Latency normalized to 42ms and 502 error rate dropped to 0.00% within 15 seconds.
attempts.engineer_notes: Identified port mismatch in Helm chart values between deployment.yaml and service.yaml.

root_cause: Incorrect upstream configuration in Nginx ingress pointing to targetPort 8080 while container was listening on 8000.
successful_fix: Correct upstream configuration and targetPort mapping in Ingress ConfigMap.
engineer_feedback: Service restart was a reflexive mistake that wasted 10 minutes. Upstream config should have been checked first.

title: 502 Bad Gateway on Checkout Service after canary rollout
error_message: 502 Bad Gateway: connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream
symptoms: Canary traffic hitting 502 errors on POST /checkout/orders. Error rate spiked to 35%.
logs: [error] 4812#0: *44102 connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream, client: 203.0.113.88, request: "POST /checkout/orders", upstream: "http://10.244.3.44:3000"
infrastructure_details: Envoy Service Mesh -> Node.js Cluster
additional_context: Canary pod spec was updated with an environment variable for host binding.

attempts.action: Restart Checkout canary pods
attempts.hypothesis: Node.js app crashed on startup
attempts.failure_reason: Pods restarted into Running state but Envoy continued returning 502 Connection refused.
attempts.observed_result: App was running, but rejecting ingress connections.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting the app did not fix the connection refusal.

attempts.action: Correct upstream host binding configuration from 127.0.0.1 to 0.0.0.0
attempts.hypothesis: New Node.js server version bound to localhost instead of all interfaces.
attempts.observed_result: Traffic immediately accepted by pod. 502s dropped to zero.
attempts.engineer_notes: Upstream listener configuration was restricting connections outside the container.

root_cause: Node.js v3.1.0 default HOST bound to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, rejecting container networking.
successful_fix: Correct upstream listener configuration (HOST=0.0.0.0).
engineer_feedback: Restarting was attempted first, which failed. The upstream binding was the issue.

title: Intermittent 502 Bad Gateway on User Gateway

symptoms: 15% of auth token validation calls failing with 502.

attempts.failure_reason: Timeout change caused Nginx to hang longer on dead pods, worsening 502 cascade.
attempts.observed_result: 502 errors increased to 22%.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing timeout caused backpressure on clients.

attempts.action: Fix upstream max_fails and fail_timeout configuration in NGINX

attempts.engineer_notes: Adjusted max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s.

successful_fix: Correct upstream Nginx fail_timeout and max_fails configuration.
engineer_feedback: Increasing timeout failed. Correcting the upstream parameters worked immediately.

title: PostgreSQL Connection Pool Exhaustion in Order Management
error_message: org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections
symptoms: Order placement stalling. Database CPU at 30% but connection count pinned at 200/200 max connections.
logs:
HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.
FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved for non-replication superuser connections
infrastructure_details: AWS Aurora PostgreSQL 15.3, PgBouncer proxy
additional_context: Followed an email flash-sale broadcast campaign.

attempts.action: Restart Order Management application pods
attempts.hypothesis: Application connection leak holding open dead JDBC sockets
attempts.failure_reason: Upon pod restart, 40 pods simultaneously attempted to reopen 20 connections each, immediately overwhelming Aurora again.
attempts.observed_result: Connections instantly pegged at 200 again in under 10 seconds.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting the app exacerbated the connection thundering herd.

attempts.action: Increase HikariCP connectionTimeout from 30s to 120s
attempts.hypothesis: Allowing threads to wait longer will smooth queue bursts
attempts.failure_reason: Tomcat worker threads became starved waiting on JDBC connections, resulting in client HTTP 504 Gateway Timeouts.
attempts.observed_result: Application became unresponsive; memory consumption rose due to thread backlog.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing connection timeout transformed connection errors into widespread thread starvation.

attempts.action: Switch PgBouncer to transaction pooling mode and tune max_client_conn
attempts.hypothesis: Session-level pooling in PgBouncer was pinning physical Aurora connections to idle client sessions.
attempts.observed_result: Active Aurora connections dropped from 200 to 28 while serving 1,400 concurrent clients.
attempts.engineer_notes: Transaction pooling multiplexed connections efficiently across order requests.

root_cause: PgBouncer configured with pool_mode=session held backend connections during idle client network round-trips.
successful_fix: Enable PgBouncer transaction pooling mode and cap per-pod HikariCP pool size to 10.
engineer_feedback: Restarting services made the outage worse due to thundering herd. Pool tuning was the only real fix.

title: MySQL Deadlock Cascade in Inventory Reservation
error_message: Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction (1213)
symptoms: Cart checkout failures spiking to 28%. Lock wait timeout exceeded errors appearing in logs.
logs:
ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
*** (1) WAITING FOR THIS LOCK TO BE GRANTED: RECORD LOCKS space id 42 page no 12 n bits 72 index `PRIMARY` of table `inventory`
infrastructure_details: MySQL 8.0 InnoDB RDS cluster
additional_context: High concurrency on top-selling SKU items.

attempts.action: Increase innodb_lock_wait_timeout from 5s to 30s
attempts.hypothesis: Transactions will succeed if allowed more time to acquire row locks
attempts.failure_reason: Transactions held locks longer, causing waiting lock queues to explode from 15 to 240, triggering system stall.
attempts.observed_result: Throughput plummeted 80%.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing lock timeout worsened the lock contention queue.

attempts.action: Sort SKU lock acquisition order lexicographically in reservation query
attempts.hypothesis: Deadlocks occurred because concurrent workers locked SKU items in arbitrary non-deterministic order.
attempts.observed_result: Deadlocks dropped to zero; transaction latency stabilized at 18ms.
attempts.engineer_notes: Deterministic lock ordering mathematically eliminates cyclic wait deadlocks.

root_cause: Unsorted multi-row UPDATE statements creating cyclic InnoDB row lock acquisition dependencies.
successful_fix: Enforce deterministic sorting of entity IDs before executing batch locks in transaction.
engineer_feedback: Lock timeout tweaking failed. Lock ordering resolved it permanently.

title: Auth Token Signature Verification Failure after JWKS Key Rotation
error_message: JWT::InvalidSignature: Key ID (kid) not found in JWKS cache
symptoms: 100% of user API requests rejected with HTTP 401 Unauthorized across mobile and web clients.
logs: ERROR [auth.jwt] Token verification failed: Key ID 'auth-key-2026-09' not present in cached JWKS provider response. Remote JWKS fetch failed with 429 Too Many Requests.
infrastructure_details: Auth0 Identity Provider -> API Gateway JWT Verifier
additional_context: Scheduled IdP key rotation executed at 09:00 UTC.

attempts.action: Restart API Gateway instances
attempts.hypothesis: Clear in-memory corrupted token cache
attempts.failure_reason: Restarting caused hundreds of API Gateway worker threads to simultaneously hit the IdP JWKS endpoint, triggering HTTP 429 Rate Limiting.
attempts.observed_result: Jwks endpoint returned 429, leaving the cache completely empty.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting the gateway turned a cache miss into a severe rate-limit lockout.

attempts.action: Warm JWKS public keys via Redis shared cache with exponential backoff
attempts.hypothesis: Provide a centralized cached key store with circuit breaker to avoid hitting IdP rate limits.
attempts.observed_result: Gateways read valid JWKS key from Redis; 401 errors ceased within 10 seconds.
attempts.engineer_notes: Shared key cache with background refresh prevented downstream IdP rate limits.

root_cause: API Gateway lacked centralized JWKS caching; IdP key rotation triggered thundering herd HTTP 429 from Auth0.
successful_fix: Inject current public key into shared Redis JWKS cache and enable stale-while-revalidate.
engineer_feedback: Service restart was disastrous due to IdP rate limits. Cache pre-warming was the correct solution.

title: OAuth Token Expiry Spike due to NTP Clock Skew
error_message: JWT::ImmatureSignature: Current time is earlier than token issued-at (nbf/iat)
symptoms: Intermittent 401 errors for freshly generated user tokens on 2 worker nodes.
logs: WARN [oauth.validator] Token iat 1792341605 is in future relative to node clock 1792341570 (delta: -35s)
infrastructure_details: AWS EC2 AutoScaling Group, chrony NTP daemon
additional_context: Followed an AWS infrastructure host retirement event.

attempts.action: Increase JWT expiration window in application config
attempts.hypothesis: Tokens expiring prematurely before client arrival
attempts.failure_reason: Tokens failed not because they expired, but because they were deemed 'not yet valid' (future iat timestamp).
attempts.observed_result: 401 errors continued unchanged.
attempts.engineer_notes: Changing token expiration did nothing for future timestamp errors.

attempts.action: Force NTP resynchronization via chronyd on drifted EC2 instances and configure clock leeway
attempts.hypothesis: Host clock had drifted 35 seconds backwards following hypervisor live migration.
attempts.observed_result: Clock offset reduced to 0.12ms; all token verifications passed.
attempts.engineer_notes: Set token verification leeway to 60s as defense-in-depth.

root_cause: Virtualization host drift caused 35-second backward clock skew on 2 instances, violating JWT issued-at validation.
successful_fix: Resynchronize NTP with chronyd and configure 60-second clock skew leeway in JWT verifier.
engineer_feedback: Configuring expiration duration failed. NTP sync plus verification leeway was the fix.

title: Node.js Event Listener Memory Leak in Notification Worker
error_message: FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
symptoms: Notification pods crashing every 45 minutes with exit code 137. Delivery latency climbing from 200ms to 45s.
logs:
<--- JS stacktrace --->
FATAL ERROR: Reached heap limit Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 1011 connection listeners added to [Socket].
infrastructure_details: Kubernetes Deployment, 2GB memory limit per pod
additional_context: Introduced in recent PR adding WebSocket connection retries.

attempts.action: Increase pod memory limit from 2Gi to 4Gi
attempts.hypothesis: Give application more headroom during traffic spikes
attempts.failure_reason: Pod survived for 90 minutes instead of 45 minutes, but heap still grew monotonically until OOMKilled at 4Gi.
attempts.observed_result: Merely delayed the inevitable crash while consuming double the cloud cluster resources.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing memory limits is a classic anti-pattern for unbound listener leaks.

attempts.action: Patch WebSocket reconnect handler to remove dangling event listeners on socket close
attempts.hypothesis: Each reconnect created a new 'error' and 'data' listener on the singleton socket without removing old ones.
attempts.observed_result: Heap plateaued at stable 180MB across 24 hours under peak load.
attempts.engineer_notes: Removed dangling event listeners using socket.off() in cleanup hook.

root_cause: WebSocket reconnection loop appended new event listeners on every retry without removing previous callbacks.
successful_fix: Add socket.removeAllListeners() in reconnection cleanup cycle.
engineer_feedback: Increasing memory limit was a futile waste of time. Removing event listeners fixed the leak.

title: JVM Metaspace Leak in Analytics Reporting Service
error_message: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
symptoms: Service stops serving GraphQL requests after running for 6 hours; JVM crashes with OutOfMemoryError.
logs:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
[GC (Metadata GC Threshold) [Metaspace: 256120K->256120K(1085440K)]]
infrastructure_details: Java 21 Spring Boot on AWS Fargate
additional_context: Frequent dynamic Groovy script evaluations for custom customer reports.

attempts.action: Increase JVM heap size (-Xmx4g)
attempts.hypothesis: Heap exhaustion during large dataset aggregations
attempts.failure_reason: Metaspace is stored in native memory outside the standard Java object heap. -Xmx has zero effect on Metaspace.
attempts.observed_result: Crash occurred at the exact same threshold.
attempts.engineer_notes: Tuning heap size demonstrates misunderstanding of Metaspace classloader dynamics.

attempts.action: Enable GroovyClassLoader script caching and compile reuse
attempts.hypothesis: Every incoming report recompiled dynamic scripts into unique generated classes, saturating Metaspace.
attempts.observed_result: Metaspace usage stabilized at 84MB.
attempts.engineer_notes: Cached compiled script classes using GroovyClassLoader.parseClass(GroovyCodeSource).

root_cause: Dynamic Groovy script execution spawned uncached classloaders, consuming all allocated Metaspace.
successful_fix: Implement LRU compiled script cache with shared GroovyClassLoader.
engineer_feedback: Adjusting -Xmx was useless. Caching the generated script classes resolved the leak.

title: Redis Connection Timeouts during Spike in Session Store
error_message: Redis::TimeoutError: Connection timed out - [Redis:6379] after 1000ms
symptoms: User logins failing with session timeout errors. Redis CPU pegged at 100% on master node.
logs:
Redis::TimeoutError: Connection timed out - [redis.cache.internal:6379] command: GET sess:918237
[SLOWLOG] 1) 1791989100 2) 421900us 3) KEYS sess:user:* 4) 10.0.8.21:44102
infrastructure_details: Redis 7.2 Cluster AWS ElastiCache, 3 shards, 1 replica each
additional_context: Background batch job launched by marketing analytics team.

attempts.action: Restart Redis cluster nodes
attempts.hypothesis: Redis engine stuck in hung event loop
attempts.failure_reason: Failover triggered slave promotion, but analytics job immediately resumed querying KEYS on the new master, pegging CPU at 100% again.
attempts.observed_result: Outage resumed within 20 seconds of failover.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting Redis master caused unnecessary replica re-sync without stopping the offending query.

attempts.action: Increase Redis command timeout in application client to 5000ms
attempts.hypothesis: Allow application to wait for Redis to catch up
attempts.failure_reason: All web worker threads became blocked waiting for Redis replies, exhausting Puma thread pool.
attempts.observed_result: Web server stopped answering health checks and was terminated by ALB.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing timeout caused catastrophic cascading failure to the upstream web tier.

attempts.action: Kill blocking KEYS command via CLIENT KILL and replace with non-blocking SCAN in analytics query
attempts.hypothesis: O(N) KEYS command blocked single-threaded Redis event loop for 420ms per execution.
attempts.observed_result: Redis CPU dropped from 100% to 8%; session read latency dropped to 0.4ms.
attempts.engineer_notes: Blocked KEYS command was identified via SLOWLOG GET 10.

root_cause: Analytics script executed blocking KEYS sess:user:* across 12 million keys on single-threaded Redis master.
successful_fix: Kill blocking client connection, rename KEYS command in redis.conf, and migrate script to cursor-based SCAN.
engineer_feedback: Restarting Redis and increasing timeouts both failed miserably. Killing the blocking KEYS query solved it.

attempts.observed_result: Connected clients stabilized at 400 total connections; autocomplete latency returned to 3ms.
attempts.engineer_notes: Injected shared singleton ConnectionPool into FastAPI app state.

title: Kafka Consumer Group Rebalance Storm in Order Ingestion
error_message: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CommitFailedException: Commit cannot be completed since the group has already rebalanced
symptoms: Message processing lag on orders-topic grew from 100 messages to 450,000 messages in 20 minutes.
logs:

Member order-worker-7f4b sent heartbeat after max.poll.interval.ms exceeded.
infrastructure_details: Confluent Kafka 7.5 cluster, 32 partitions on orders-topic
additional_context: Large batch order payloads with external credit check API calls.

attempts.action: Restart consumer group pods
attempts.hypothesis: Clear hung Kafka consumer threads
attempts.failure_reason: Pod termination and recreation triggered another catastrophic cascade of group rebalances, pausing all consumption.
attempts.observed_result: Consumer lag accelerated to 750,000 messages.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting pods during a rebalance storm is like pouring gasoline on a fire.

attempts.action: Increase max.poll.interval.ms from 300000 to 900000 and reduce max.poll.records to 25

attempts.observed_result: Rebalances stopped completely; consumer group processed backlog at 12,000 msg/sec.

successful_fix: Increase max.poll.interval.ms to 15m and reduce max.poll.records to 25.

title: Poison Pill Dead-Letter Starvation in Payment Webhook Queue
error_message: JSON::ParserError: 784: unexpected token at '<<MALFORMED_XML_PAYLOAD>>'
symptoms: Webhook queue consumer stuck on partition 3; 18,000 valid merchant webhooks delayed.
logs: ERROR [consumer.rb:48] Failed to deserialize message offset 891024 on webhook-events: JSON::ParserError. Retrying immediately...
infrastructure_details: RabbitMQ / SQS queue processor
additional_context: Legacy third-party merchant sent legacy XML payload to JSON endpoint.

attempts.action: Restart Webhook Ingestion service
attempts.hypothesis: Flush corrupted memory state
attempts.failure_reason: Consumer immediately picked up the exact same un-acknowledged poison pill message and threw JSON::ParserError again.
attempts.observed_result: Queue remained blocked at the exact same offset.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting does not advance an unacknowledged queue message.

attempts.action: Route deserialization failures to Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) after 3 retries
attempts.hypothesis: Malformed payloads should be isolated to DLQ without halting head-of-line processing.
attempts.observed_result: Poison message routed to DLQ; backlog of 18,000 pending webhooks drained in 45 seconds.
attempts.engineer_notes: Wrapped deserializer in try/catch with DLQ forwarder.

root_cause: Consumer lacked Dead Letter Queue logic; infinite retry loop on unparseable payload caused head-of-line blocking.
successful_fix: Add try/catch exception routing to Dead Letter Queue with alert metric.
engineer_feedback: Service restart failed. Implementing DLQ routing cleared the queue instantly.

title: CoreDNS Throttling and ndots:5 Query Amplification

title: cgroup v2 Memory Limit Miscalculation and Container OOMKilled
error_message: OOMKilled: Exit Code 137, Container killed by Linux Out Of Memory Killer
symptoms: High-throughput machine learning inference pod crashing every 10 minutes under model loading.
logs:
kernel: [18920.12] Memory cgroup out of memory: Kill process 29101 (python) score 1012 or sacrifice child
Pod status: Terminated (Reason: OOMKilled, ExitCode: 137)
infrastructure_details: Kubernetes 1.29 on Ubuntu 22.04 with cgroup v2
additional_context: Upgraded cluster worker nodes from cgroup v1 to v2.

attempts.action: Restart recommendation engine deployment
attempts.hypothesis: Temporary burst in inference request queue
attempts.failure_reason: Upon startup, PyTorch pre-allocated CUDA pinned host memory which instantly hit the 4Gi cgroup limit.
attempts.observed_result: Pod was OOMKilled within 90 seconds of startup.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting resulted in an immediate CrashLoopBackOff cycle.

attempts.action: Adjust memory limits in pod spec to 8Gi and enable PyTorch memory fragmentation allocator config
attempts.hypothesis: Model weights required 3.8GB baseline memory; page cache overhead triggered the cgroup v2 hard limit.
attempts.observed_result: Container memory stabilized at 5.1GB without OOM events.
attempts.engineer_notes: Set PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128.

root_cause: Container memory limit (4Gi) did not account for Linux page cache and pinned tensor memory under cgroup v2.
successful_fix: Increase container memory limit to 8Gi and set PyTorch allocator tuning.
engineer_feedback: Restarting the pod was useless. Right-sizing the cgroup limit and allocator resolved the crash.

logs:
ClientError: An error occurred (SlowDown) when calling the PutObject operation: Please reduce your request rate.
Target key: exports/2026-08-30/invoice_batch_001.pdf
infrastructure_details: AWS S3 bucket us-east-1, multi-threaded Celery workers
additional_context: End-of-month financial reconciliation run.

attempts.action: Increase Celery concurrency workers from 20 to 60
attempts.hypothesis: Speed up processing by throwing more workers at the task
attempts.failure_reason: Adding more concurrent workers dramatically amplified the PutObject request rate to the single prefix, pushing SlowDown rate to 95%.
attempts.observed_result: Total batch failure.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing concurrency against a throttled partition is counter-productive.

attempts.action: Prefix S3 object keys with hex hash and configure exponential jittered backoff in boto3 config
attempts.hypothesis: S3 partitions prefixes automatically; single sequential date prefix concentrated all 5,000 req/sec onto one partition.
attempts.observed_result: Requests distributed across multiple S3 partition shards; SlowDown errors dropped to 0.
attempts.engineer_notes: Implemented key format: exports/{md5_hash[:4]}/{date}/...

root_cause: Single prefix in S3 bucket exceeded the 3,500 PUT/second per partition limit due to un-partitioned date key format.
successful_fix: Distribute S3 object keys with random prefix hash and enable adaptive client-side retry mode.
engineer_feedback: Scaling up workers made it worse. Key partitioning and backoff resolved it.

title: Gunicorn Sync Worker Timeout during File Upload Bursts
error_message: [CRITICAL] WORKER TIMEOUT (pid:4918)
symptoms: File uploads failing with 504 Gateway Timeout. Gunicorn master continuously killing and restarting workers.
infrastructure_details: Gunicorn with default sync worker class, Nginx reverse proxy
additional_context: Clients on slow mobile networks uploading high-resolution photos.

attempts.action: Increase Gunicorn --timeout from 30s to 180s
attempts.hypothesis: Give slow uploads more time before master terminates worker
attempts.failure_reason: Synchronous workers remained occupied for 180s per slow client; all 8 worker slots became instantly exhausted, locking out all other traffic.
attempts.observed_result: Service completely stopped responding to all requests.
attempts.engineer_notes: Increasing timeout on sync workers causes complete starvation of available worker slots.

attempts.action: Switch Gunicorn worker class to uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker (async) and enable client buffering in Nginx
attempts.hypothesis: Async event-loop handles slow network I/O non-blockingly without holding worker threads captive.
attempts.observed_result: Zero worker timeouts; system handled 1,200 concurrent uploads smoothly.
attempts.engineer_notes: Changed command to: gunicorn -k uvicorn.workers.UvicornWorker main:app.

root_cause: Gunicorn sync workers held captive by slow client upload network transfer speeds.
successful_fix: Switch to asynchronous Uvicorn worker class and enable Nginx request body buffering.
engineer_feedback: Increasing timeout caused total worker starvation. Switching to async workers solved it.

title: TLS Handshake Failure due to Intermediate Certificate Expiration
error_message: SSL_ERROR_UNTRUSTED_ISSUER: The certificate issuer's certificate has expired
symptoms: Browser clients reporting untrusted certificate warning; mobile apps failing SSL pinning checks.
logs: nginx: [crit] 19#19: *8820 SSL_do_handshake() failed (SSL: error:0A000086:SSL routines::certificate verify failed:issuer has expired)
infrastructure_details: Nginx Ingress with cert-manager Let's Encrypt
additional_context: Intermediate R3 certificate transition by Certificate Authority.

attempts.action: Restart Ingress Controller pods
attempts.hypothesis: Reload in-memory TLS certificate cache
attempts.failure_reason: Pods reloaded the exact same expired intermediate certificate chain from the existing Kubernetes Secret.
attempts.observed_result: SSL error remained active on all client handshakes.
attempts.engineer_notes: Restarting ingress controllers does not update the underlying secret.

attempts.action: Regenerate full certificate chain with updated cross-signed root via cert-manager
attempts.hypothesis: Leaf cert was valid but bundled intermediate certificate had expired.
attempts.observed_result: Certificate chain verified by openssl s_client; client handshakes succeeded immediately.
attempts.engineer_notes: cert-manager renew --force with preferredChain='ISRG Root X1'.

root_cause: Kubernetes TLS Secret bundled an expired intermediate cross-signed certificate authority chain.
successful_fix: Renew full chain with updated cross-signed root and trigger ingress cert reload.
engineer_feedback: Restarting pods was useless. Renewing the cert-manager certificate chain solved it.
